messages.subject_clean: Interpreting coefficients with exploratory Extended Mixed-Effect Item Response Model
messages.body_plain:
The exploratory model would be hard to interpret here because the orientation of the loadings is arbitrary (fixed at a particular orthogonal configuration during estimation). You could probably interpret the fixed-effect intercept terms as is, but loading coefficients are subject to post-rotation. In general, it's better to use this methodology with known factor structure configurations.

Phil

On Sat, Aug 5, 2017 at 9:31 AM, <bruno....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Phil,

> I am currently working on an adaptive intelligence test.
>
> I always thought that specific objectivity or sample independence is a necessary condition for adaptive testing,
>
> because only if the rank of the item difficulty is the same for all respondents independent of ability, and
>
> the rank of the person ability is the same for items independently of difficulty,
>
> it does not matter which item of the item pool is used.
>

>
> But there are a lot of books and papers describing a 2PL or 3PL adaptive test.
>
> So my question is: How do I argue that. Why am I allowed to use a 2PL or 3PL?

Sample independence is something that should hold for all IRT models, though specific objectivity only for Rasch models. I personally find specific objectively more of a buzz-word than something practically useful.

When fitting statistical models to empirical data, we generally want models that reflect the properties of the data, which Rasch models often will not accomplish (e.g., accounting for guessing, noticing that some items seem to separate lower/higher individuals better than others, including information about the distractor items, etc). Ignoring these properties can lead to improper inferences about the latent traits, which is generally why more flexible response models are used in practice.

That's not to say you couldn't build a CAT with just Rasch items. Doing so means that you are selecting items that match the latent ability right at the inflection points, which in this case is identical to picking items with "maximum information" given some provisional ability estimate. From a CAT perspective though, we're typically more interested in building realistic adaptive tests that reflect empirical properties inherent in testing situations rather than building some situation specific (and largely unverifiable) specific objectivity measure. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: specific objectivity & adaptive testing
messages.subject_clean: specific objectivity & adaptive testing
messages.body_plain:
In addition to the philosophical Rasch v. more parameters, there may be some practical issues to consider. Selecting a model may also depend largely on your sample size for calibration and what your testing program can support now and in the future.

On Tuesday, August 8, 2017 at 6:46:08 AM UTC-4, Phil Chalmers wrote:

> On Sat, Aug 5, 2017 at 9:31 AM, <bruno....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Phil,
> >
> >
> >
> > I am currently working on an adaptive intelligence test.
> >
> > I always thought that specific objectivity or sample independence is a necessary condition for adaptive testing,
> >
> > because only if the rank of the item difficulty is the same for all respondents independent of ability, and
> >
> > the rank of the person ability is the same for items independently of difficulty,
> >
> > it does not matter which item of the item pool is used.
> >
> >
> >
> > But there are a lot of books and papers describing a 2PL or 3PL adaptive test.
> >
> > So my question is: How do I argue that. Why am I allowed to use a 2PL or 3PL?
>
> Sample independence is something that should hold for all IRT models, though specific objectivity only for Rasch models. I personally find specific objectively more of a buzz-word than something practically useful.
>
> When fitting statistical models to empirical data, we generally want models that reflect the properties of the data, which Rasch models often will not accomplish (e.g., accounting for guessing, noticing that some items seem to separate lower/higher individuals better than others, including information about the distractor items, etc). Ignoring these properties can lead to improper inferences about the latent traits, which is generally why more flexible response models are used in practice.
>
> That's not to say you couldn't build a CAT with just Rasch items. Doing so means that you are selecting items that match the latent ability right at the inflection points, which in this case is identical to picking items with "maximum information" given some provisional ability estimate. From a CAT perspective though, we're typically more interested in building realistic adaptive tests that reflect empirical properties inherent in testing situations rather than building some situation specific (and largely unverifiable) specific objectivity measure. HTH.
>
> Phil
>
>

> >
> > Best regards, Bruno

messages.body_plain:
Here is the code use to estimate the RSM and to generate the Wright Map in 'mirt:'

mod1 <- mirt(resp, model=1, itemtype="rsm")
mod1
theta <- fscores(mod1, full.scores = TRUE, method = "ML")
hist(theta)
summary(mod1)
# Wright Map
b <- sapply(1:ncol(resp), function(i) coef(mod1)[[i]][, "c"])
wrightMap(theta, b, item.side = itemClassic)

Attached to this you will find a screen shot of the plot generated.

For comparison, here is the code used to generate the Wright Map in 'TAM:'

mod01 <- tam.mml(resp, constrain="persons", irtmodel="RSM", pid = dat_sub$ai_code_13, control=list(maxiter=1000, increment.factor=1.02))

xsi <- mod01$xsi
delta <- mod01$xsi
delta <- as.data.frame(delta[1:22, ])
ability <- tam.wle(mod01, WLE=FALSE)
wrightMap(ability$theta, delta$xsi, item.side = itemClassic)

Both ability estimates have been generated with ML.

messages.body_plain:
Because mirt estimates models with the slope intercept format, not the classical IRT discrimination/difficulty parameterization (which is known to be unstable). So transforming b = -d/a is required, but since a = 1 for Rasch models then you just end up multiplying by -1.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Shuffling in new questions to mirtCAT session
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for posting on the forum, Elliott. This is indeed a tricky question, because there are many variables that should be considered, such as whether the CAT session should still be adaptive, when to terminate the test in light of new (unscored) items, when/how many new items each person should receive, etc.

To demonstrate the core concepts of this problem, I generated a new vignette on the wiki, located here: http://philchalmers.github.io/mirtCAT/html/unidim-newitems.html
This shows how to add two new unscored items to an existing bank, while ensuring that the items in the calibrated bank are still selected using the maximum-information criteria. I hope it helps highlight what needs to be done, and why setting up this data collection scheme can be a bit awkward (at first; after you see the result it isn't that bad or counter-intuitive). Cheers.

Phil

Charlie

Dear Chalmers,
I have the same problem with Hend. I need to compare the ability of different dimensions in a three dimension mirt model.
How can I obtain the non-standardized scores of persons in each dimension ?
Can fscores() do that?
The following is my R program:

library("mirt")
setwd('~/My_R')
# data
D27 <- read.csv("all27.csv")
# the confirmatory model:
mod1.mixed27<-mirt.model
('
F1 = 1,6,9,13,14,17,19,21,23
F2 = 2,3,4,7,8,10,15,16,18,20,24,25,27
F3 = 5,11,12,22,26
START = (14,a1,1.0),(2,a2,1.0),(5,a3,1.0)
FIXED = (14,a1),(2,a2),(5,a3)
COV = F1*F2*F3
')
# data types
mixed.types <- rep("gpcm", 27)
mixed.types[3]  <- "2PL"
mixed.types[11] <- "2PL"
mixed.types[21] <- "2PL"

mod1.27 <- mirt(D27, mod1.mixed27, itemtype = mixed.types, method = 'MHRM')

coef1.27.sim <- coef(mod1.27, simplify=TRUE)
write.csv(coef1.27.sim$items, file="coef1_27_sim__iterms.csv")
mod1.27.abil <- fscores(mod1.27, QMC = TRUE)
write.csv(mod1.27.abil, file="mod1_27_abil.csv")

Thanks
Max Wu
